V is the Latin form of a letter that came from the Greek upsilon. Latin used it for both the u vowel and a w-like consonant, and U and W both grew out of it later, which is why the three letters still sit together in the alphabet.

If you want a lowercase-height V for a small-caps name, Unicode has ᴠ, which you can copy straight from this sentence. It pairs well with other small capitals.

pages.letter_notes:
W says its own origin out loud: in English its name is "double u", and it began as two V or U shapes written side by side. It is one of the youngest letters in the Latin alphabet, added long after the Romans to write a sound that Latin did not have but the Germanic languages needed.

Because W is two letters fused together, the decorative rows can get busy. The blackletter 𝔚 and 𝖂 pack a lot of strokes into one character, which looks dramatic as an initial but can crowd a longer name. The Sans-Serif 𝖶 and Monospace 𝚆 keep it clean, and the Fullwidth Ｗ sits in a wide cell, so it puts extra space around a short name. Nothing in the W grid is borrowed, so you can mix rows freely. The script rows, 𝒲 and 𝓦, turn the four strokes into a looping shape that suits an elegant display name, and the Circled Ⓦ fits all four strokes inside a ring.

pages.letter_notes:
Unicode has a small capital form for every other letter of the alphabet, but there is no small capital X. If you are building a name in small caps, X is the one gap to plan around: a regular lowercase x usually sits at the same height and is the simplest swap.

Latin took X from the Greek alphabet and used it for the ks sound, which is still its job in words like box and six. It is one of the few letters that spells two sounds at once.

No X in the grid is borrowed. Because the letter is symmetrical, the slanted rows change it more than you might expect: Italic 𝑋 and Sans Italic 𝘟 tilt both strokes, so the crossing point shifts. The Gothic 𝔛 and Bold Gothic 𝖃 turn the simple cross into a much more ornate blackletter shape. For a sharp, minimal X, the Sans Bold 𝗫 and Monospace 𝚇 keep the two strokes straight and even.

pages.letter_notes:
Why do French speakers call Y "i grec", and Spanish speakers "i griega", the Greek i? The Romans borrowed the letter from the Greek upsilon so they could spell words taken from Greek, and that origin stuck in the name in both languages.

Nothing on this page is borrowed for Y. The tail is what changes most between styles. The script rows, Cursive Light 𝒴 and Cursive Bold 𝓨, give it a long sweep below the line, while the Monospace 𝚈 and Sans-Serif 𝖸 keep the arms short and even, and the Fullwidth Ｙ gives the fork extra room. The Gothic 𝔜 and Bold Gothic 𝖄 are the least like a plain Y, so they work better as a single initial than inside a long name. Unicode also has a small capital ʏ, which you can take straight from this paragraph if your name uses small caps. Pair it with other small capitals rather than full-size letters so the line stays even.

pages.letter_notes:
ℨ and ℤ, in the Gothic and Double-Struck rows, are both borrowed. They paste as ordinary text, so a name ending in Z works the same way in either style. The script rows, Cursive Light 𝒵 and Cursive Bold 𝓩, need no stand-ins, and neither does the Bold Gothic 𝖅, which means a heavy blackletter Z stays in one consistent alphabet with the rest of a name. Bold 𝐙 and the italic rows also come straight from their own alphabets.

Z sits at the end of the alphabet because the Romans added it late. They borrowed it from the Greek zeta, which itself came from the Phoenician zayin, mainly so they could spell words taken from Greek, and placed it after the letters they already had. That late arrival explains its position, even though zeta sat much earlier in the Greek alphabet. Today Z is the final letter in English, and the last stop on this A to Z list.
